title: Build Local AI Apps with C++ and NVIDIA TensorRT RTX Samples | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's open-source DIN Deploy C++ samples pair ONNX Runtime with the TensorRT RTX execution provider for local ASR, segmentation and image generation, with DGX Spark GPU speedups of roughly 12-77x over CPU. Largely a developer-promotion piece reinforcing NVIDIA's client-side inference stack.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's open-source Do Inference Now (DIN) Deploy collection provides C++ samples combining ONNX Runtime with the NVIDIA TensorRT RTX execution provider to take a model checkpoint to a native, hardware-accelerated app on Windows and Linux.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is lowering the friction of shipping local AI on RTX, reinforcing its GPU software moat on the client side.
insights.locator: Do Inference Now (DIN) Deploy is an open-source collection

insights.claim: Each DIN Deploy sample splits a Python exporter (Hugging Face checkpoint to ONNX) from a native C++ CLI on ONNX Runtime, so deployment needs no model-specific runtime.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Portable ONNX artifacts decouple model choice from runtime, favoring whichever vendor supplies the best execution provider.
insights.locator: From ONNX export to C++ implementation

insights.claim: Most sample code uses only ONNX Runtime session and tensor APIs; CUDA APIs and kernels appear only in optional accelerated paths, so other execution providers supporting the required tensor APIs can run the shared code.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Vendor-neutral shared code lowers lock-in, but NVIDIA's accelerated paths remain the performance showcase.
insights.locator: Most sample code uses ONNX Runtime session and tensor APIs

insights.claim: The same ONNX Runtime API can be accessed through WinML 2.0, and the repository ships CMake presets for Windows, Linux, x86-64 and Arm64, with DirectX available only on Windows.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Arm64 and WinML support signals NVIDIA targeting Windows-on-Arm and mainstream Windows app developers.

insights.claim: DIN Deploy covers offline and streaming speech recognition using OpenAI Whisper, NVIDIA Parakeet TDT and NVIDIA Nemotron ASR Streaming.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: NVIDIA promotes its own open ASR models alongside Whisper as local-inference defaults.
insights.locator: AI tasks supported by DIN Deploy

insights.claim: Meta SAM 2.1 samples provide interactive masking for images and video, and FLUX.2-klein-4B provides prompt-driven image generation.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Samples span speech, segmentation and generation, the core workloads for on-device AI apps.
insights.locator: Meta SAM 2.1 samples support interactive masking

insights.claim: On DGX Spark, GPU vs CPU speeds were: whisper-large-v3-turbo 58.5x vs 3.8x real time, nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b 39.01x vs 3.24x, and parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 206.41x vs 14.44x.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: GPU gives roughly 12-15x over CPU on speech workloads, supporting the case for GPU-accelerated local AI.
insights.locator: Table 1 compares GPU and CPU performance

insights.claim: Meta SAM 2.1 (hiera-base-plus) runs at 38.3 FPS on the DGX Spark GPU versus 0.5 FPS on CPU, about a 77x gap.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Vision segmentation is far more GPU-dependent than ASR, so real-time vision on-device effectively requires a GPU.

insights.claim: The FLUX.2 sample uses ONNX Runtime 1.25 graphics interop with Vulkan and DirectX, letting applications integrate GPU-resident resources with a cross-vendor shader interface.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Tighter pairing of AI inference and graphics pipelines matters for games and creative-app vendors.

insights.claim: Post-training quantization with NVIDIA Model Optimizer yields a quantized ONNX model that is a drop-in replacement requiring no application-code changes, though quantization is hardware-dependent.
insights.speaker: Luca Spindler
insights.so_what: Easy quantization drives adoption of recent tensor-core hardware, as the post says it can drastically accelerate models.
